source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΕΓΚΩΜΙΑΣΤΙΚΗ. Εἰς τὸν ἅγιον μάρτυρα Λουκιανόν. αʹ. Ὅπερ χθὲς ἐδεδοίκειν ἐξέβη, καὶ τέλος ἔλαβε νῦν, καὶ τῆς ἑορτῆς ἀπελθούσης, καὶ τὸ πλῆθος ἡμῖν συν απεδήμησε, καὶ ἐλάττων ἡμῖν ὁ σύλλογος γέγονε. Καὶ ᾔδειν μὲν τοῦτο συμβησόμενον πάντως· οὐ μὴν δὲ διὰ τοῦτο τῆς παραινέσεως ἀπέστην· εἰ γὰρ καὶ μὴ πάντες ἐπείσθησαν οἱ χθὲς ἀκούσαντες, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ πάντες ἠπείθησαν· οὐ μικρὸν δὲ τοῦτο εἰς παραμυθίας λόγον ἡμῖν· διόπερ οὐδὲ σήμερον ἀποστήσομαι ταύτης τῆς συμβουλῆς· εἰ γὰρ καὶ μὴ δι' ἡμῶν, ἀλλά γε δι' ὑμῶν πάντως ἀκούσονται τὰ λεγόμενα. Τίς γὰρ δυνη θείη σιγῇ τὴν τοσαύτην αὐτῶν ῥᾳθυμίαν ἐνεγκεῖν, ἢ μεταδοῦναι συγγνώμης καὶ ἀπολογίας αὐτοῖς, οἳ διὰ τοσούτου χρόνου τὴν μητέρα ἰδόντες, καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ καλῶν ἀπολαύσαντες ἀπέστησαν, καὶ οὐκ ἠνέσχοντο τὸ δεύτερον ἐπιστρέψαι πάλιν, οὐδὲ τὴν τοῦ Νῶε περιστερὰν, ἀλλὰ τὸν κόρακα ἐμιμήσαντο, καὶ ταῦτα τοῦ κλυδωνίου μένοντος ἔτι, καὶ τοῦ χειμῶνος ἐκείνου, καὶ χαλεπωτέρας καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐγειρομένης ζάλης, καὶ τῆς ἁγίας ταύτης κιβωτοῦ προκειμένης ἐν μέσῳ, καὶ πάντας καλούσης, καὶ πρὸς ἑαυτὴν ἐπισπωμένης, καὶ πολλὴν τοῖς καταφεύγουσι παρεχούσης τὴν ἀσφάλειαν; Οὐ γὰρ ὑδάτων, οὐδὲ κυμάτων ἐμβολὰς, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἀλογωτάτων παθῶν τὰς συνεχεῖς ἀποκρούεται ἐπαναστάσεις, καὶ φθόνον ἀναιρεῖ, καὶ ἀπόνοιαν καταστέλλει. Οὔτε γὰρ ὁ πλούσιος ἐνταῦθα τοῦ πένητος ὑπεριδεῖν δυνήσεται, ἀκούων παρὰ τῶν θείων Γραφῶν, ὅτι Πᾶσα σὰρξ χόρτος, καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπου ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου· οὔτε ὁ πένης πλουτοῦντα ἕτερον ἰδὼν βασκανίᾳ ἁλώσεται, ἀκούων καὶ αὐτὸς ἑτέρου προφήτου λέγοντος· Μὴ φοβοῦ, ὅταν πλουτήσῃ ἄνθρωπος, ἢ ὅταν πληθυνθῇ ἡ δόξα τοῦ οἴκου αὐτοῦ· ὅτι οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἀποθνήσκειν αὐτὸν λήψεται τὰ πάντα, οὐδὲ συγκαταβήσεται αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα αὐτοῦ. Τοιαύτη γὰρ τῆς εὐπορίας ταύ της ἡ φύσις· οὐ συμμεθίσταται τοῖς ἔχουσιν, οὐ συν αποδημεῖ τοῖς κεκτημένοις, οὐ παρίσταται κρινομένοις ἐκεῖ καὶ εὐθύνας ὑπέχουσιν, ἀλλ' ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου διακόπτεται πάντως· πολλοὺς δὲ καὶ πρὸ τοῦ θανάτου κατέλιπεν· ἄπιστος ἡ χρῆσις, ἀβέβαιος ἡ ἀπόλαυσις, ἐπικίνδυνος ἡ κτῆσις. Ἀλλ' οὐ τὰ τῆς ἀρετῆς τοιαῦτα, καὶ τὰ τῆς ἐλεημοσύνης· ἀλλ' ἔστιν ἄσυλος οὗτος ὁ θησαυρός. Πόθεν τοῦτο δῆλον; Ὁ περὶ τοῦ πλούτου τούτου φιλοσοφήσας καὶ εἰπὼν, ὅτι Οὐ συγκαταβήσεται αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα αὐτοῦ ὀπίσω αὐτοῦ, οὗτος καὶ περὶ τῶν τῆς ἐλεημοσύνης θησαυρῶν, τῶν ἀεὶ μενόν των καὶ μηδέποτε συλωμένων, ἐπαίδευσεν ἡμᾶς οὕτως εἰπών· Ἐσκόρπισεν, ἔδωκε τοῖς πένησιν· ἡ δι καιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. Τί τούτου παραδοξότερον γένοιτ' ἄν; Τὰ συλλεγόμενα ἀπόλλυνται, καὶ τὰ σκορπιζόμενα μένει, καὶ μάλα εἰκότως. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ὑποδέχεται, ἐκ δὲ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ χειρὸς οὐδεὶς ἁρπάζειν δύναται· τὰ δὲ ἐν ἀνθρωπίνοις ἀποτίθεται θησαυροῖς· ἔνθα πολλαῖς ὑπόκειται ταῖς ἐπιβουλαῖς, ἔνθα πολὺς ὁ φθόνος καὶ ἡ βασκανία. Μὴ τοίνυν ἀμελῇς, ἀγαπητὲ, τῆς ἐν ταῦθα διατριβῆς· κἂν γάρ τις ἀθυμία ἐνοχλῇ, ἐνταῦθα φυγαδεύεται· κἂν φροντίδες βιωτικαὶ, δραπετεύουσι· κἂν ἄλογα πάθη, σβέννυται· ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς ἀγο ρᾶς, καὶ τῶν θεάτρων, καὶ τῶν ἄλλων συλλόγων τῶν ἔξωθεν πολλὰς ἐπισυρόμενοι φροντίδας, καὶ ἀθυμίας, καὶ ψυχῆς νόσους, οἴκαδε ἀναχωροῦμεν.
thought_title: The church as ark against worldly passions and unstable wealth
orientation: John Chrysostom opens his encomium for the martyr Lucian by lamenting that after yesterday's feast the crowd has left, and he urges those present to value the church as a spiritual ark that protects against worldly passions and the instability of wealth.
pass_a_gloss: What yesterday I feared has come out, and has now reached its end, and the feast having departed, the crowd also departed with us, and the gathering has become smaller for us. And I knew that this would happen altogether; not however for this reason did I stand away from the exhortation; for even if not all who heard yesterday were persuaded, yet not all disobeyed; and this is not small for us in the way of consolation; for which reason not even today will I stand away from this counsel; for even if not through us, yet through you altogether they will hear the things said. For who could bear in silence their so great indifference, or give to them pardon and defense, who having seen their mother through so long a time, and having enjoyed the good things in her, stood away, and did not endure to turn back a second time again, nor imitated the dove of Noah, but the raven, and these things while the storm still remains, and that winter, and a more difficult squall rising each day, and this holy ark lying before in the midst, and calling all, and drawing them to itself, and providing much safety to those who flee to it? For not of waters, nor of waves does it beat off the assaults, but the continuous uprisings of the most irrational passions, and it destroys envy, and it calms down arrogance. For neither will the rich man here be able to look down on the poor man, hearing from the divine Scriptures, that All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is as the flower of grass; nor will the poor man seeing another being rich be taken by envy, hearing also himself another prophet saying: Do not fear, when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house increases; because not in his dying will he take all things, nor will his glory go down with him. For such is the nature of this wealth; it does not depart together with those who have it, it does not travel abroad together with those who possess it, it does not stand beside those being judged there and giving account, but it is cut off by death altogether; and many it left behind even before death; untrustworthy is the use, unstable is the enjoyment, dangerous is the possession. But not such are the things of virtue, and the things of almsgiving; but this treasure is unplunderable. From where is this clear? The one who practiced self-discipline about this wealth and said, that His glory will not go down after him, this one also about the treasures of almsgiving, the ones always remaining and never being plundered, taught us, having spoken thus: He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever. What could be more paradoxical than this? The things being gathered are destroyed, and the things being scattered remain, and very reasonably. For the former God receives, and from the hand of God no one is able to snatch; but the latter are stored in human treasuries; where they are subject to many plots, where envy is great and malice. Do not then neglect, beloved, the spending of time here; for even if some despondency troubles, here it is put to flight; even if worldly cares, they run away; even if irrational passions, they are quenched; but from the marketplace, and the theaters, and the other gatherings outside, dragging along many cares, and despondencies, and diseases of soul, we withdraw home.

choices.why: The term denotes a careless, negligent slackness in attending to spiritual duties; 'indifference' captures the moral failure Chrysostom laments without implying mere laziness.
ἀπόνοια here means a loss of right thinking that manifests as pride and presumption; 'arrogance' fits the contrast with envy and the rich man's attitude.

The adjective literally means 'not subject to seizure or plunder'; 'unplunderable' preserves the concrete image of a treasure that cannot be stolen, matching the following contrast with human treasuries.
Per the glossary, φιλοσοφία is rendered 'self-discipline'; the verb here means to have spoken with disciplined wisdom about wealth, so 'practiced self-discipline' keeps the glossary term's force.
The glossary mandates 'almsgiving' for ἐλεημοσύνη, emphasizing the concrete act of giving to the poor rather than a general virtue.

pass_b_english: What I feared yesterday has now come to pass and reached its end: once the feast was over, the crowd departed along with it, and our gathering has become smaller. I knew this would certainly happen, but I did not for that reason abandon my exhortation. Even if not all who heard yesterday were persuaded, neither did all disobey, and this is no small comfort to me. Therefore I will not give up this counsel today either. Even if they do not hear through me, they will certainly hear through you. Who could bear their great indifference in silence, or offer them pardon and defense? They saw their mother after so long a time, enjoyed the good things within her, and then went away. They could not bring themselves to turn back a second time. They imitated not Noah's dove but the raven—and this while the storm still rages, while that winter continues, while a harsher squall rises every day, while this holy ark stands open in the midst, calling everyone and drawing them to itself, offering great safety to all who take refuge in it. For it does not beat off floods of water or waves, but the constant assaults of the most irrational passions. It destroys envy and calms arrogance. The rich man here cannot look down on the poor man, because he hears from the divine Scriptures: 'All flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of the grass' (Isaiah 40:6). Nor will the poor man, seeing another grow rich, be seized by envy, because he too hears another prophet say: 'Do not fear when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house increases; for when he dies he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory go down with him' (Psalm 49:17-18 (LXX 48:18-19)). Such is the nature of this abundance: it does not move with those who have it, it does not travel with those who possess it, it does not stand by them when they are judged there and called to account, but it is cut off entirely by death. Many it has abandoned even before death. Its use is untrustworthy, its enjoyment unstable, its possession dangerous. But the things of virtue are not like this, nor the things of almsgiving. This treasure is unplunderable. How is this clear? The one who spoke philosophically about this wealth and said, 'His glory will not go down after him,' also taught us about the treasures of almsgiving—the treasures that remain forever and are never plundered—when he said: 'He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever' (Psalm 112:9 (LXX 111:9)). What could be more paradoxical than this? What is gathered is destroyed, and what is scattered remains—and very rightly so. For the one kind God receives, and from God's hand no one can snatch anything away. The other kind is stored in human treasuries, where it is subject to many plots, where envy and jealousy abound. Do not, then, beloved, neglect your time here. If any despondency troubles you, it is put to flight here. If worldly cares trouble you, they flee. If irrational passions trouble you, they are quenched. But from the marketplace, the theaters, and the other gatherings outside, we return home dragging with us many cares, despondencies, and diseases of the soul.
